notes.title: Start here: a MERN invoicing app read through traces and fake PRs
notes.body:
IDURAR is an open-source ERP/CRM: clients, invoices and payments, with an Express + Mongoose backend in `idurar-erp-crm/backend/` and a React + Redux frontend in `idurar-erp-crm/frontend/`. This quest uses three files from the `fable docs/` curriculum:

1. `fable docs/00-fast-track.md`: how to run it, the two known landmines in this copy, the first ten files to open, and two flows to trace.
2. `fable docs/04-code-reading-gym/02-trace-tables.md`: six tables that follow a value hop by hop from the UI to MongoDB and back.
3. `fable docs/04-code-reading-gym/04-review-katas.md`: eight fake pull requests to review against the real code.

Work with the code open. The guides cite short names such as `create.js` or `actions.js`; several files share those names, so always find the full path first (for example `backend/src/controllers/appControllers/paymentController/create.js`).

The trace tables give their own answers in each **Verify** line. Treat those as claims to check: at least one of them does not match what the code does at this commit.

excerpts.quote: Goal: by Sunday night you can run the app, trace two end-to-end flows, make one safe change

notes.title: Concept: trust boundaries and multi-step writes
notes.body:
Two ideas run through the trace tables and the katas.

**Trust boundary.** Anything the browser sends can be edited by the user, so the server must decide which values it accepts and which it derives itself. In each trace, mark the step where data crosses from client to server, then read that controller and list, field by field, what it keeps from `req.body` and what it computes on its own. Do this for `invoiceController/create.js` and `paymentController/create.js`, and note the exact HTTP status each early `return` uses.

**Several writes, no transaction.** A controller that calls Mongoose more than once can be interrupted between calls. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions, but only when the code opens a session for them. Search the controllers for `startSession` or `withTransaction`, then, for each multi-write controller, write down what state is left if the process stops after each write. Also note what each `findOneAndUpdate` filter requires, and what the code does when nothing matches.

excerpts.quote: circle the single step where a value crosses a **trust boundary**

notes.title: Concept: JWTs plus a server-side session list
notes.body:
IDURAR uses a **JSON Web Token** for authentication: the server signs a token containing the user id, the browser sends it back in an `Authorization: Bearer` header, and the server checks the signature. A signed token cannot be cancelled on its own, so IDURAR also stores every issued token in a `loggedSessions` array on the user's password document.

Trace 3 in `02-trace-tables.md` follows this from login to a protected request. Check each step against the code:

- `backend/src/controllers/middlewaresControllers/createAuthMiddleware/isValidAuthToken.js`: list every `return res.status(...)` with its status and condition, including the `catch` block.
- Look up in the `jsonwebtoken` documentation what `jwt.verify` does when a token is expired or badly signed: does it return a value or throw?
- `logout.js` in the same folder: what does it change in the database?

Then read Kata 3 in `04-review-katas.md` and decide which files a move to cookies would touch.

notes.title: The server recomputes invoice totals
notes.body:
After Joi validation, `invoiceController/create.js` walks `items`, sets each `item.total` with `calculate.multiply(quantity, price)`, sums `subTotal`, computes `taxTotal` from `taxRate`, and then writes `body.subTotal`, `body.taxTotal` and `body.total` over whatever the client sent. The saved document therefore always carries the server's numbers.

- *The client total*: Joi accepting a field does not mean the controller keeps it; it is overwritten.
- *The lower of the two*: there is no comparison between client and server totals.
- *A Mongoose total validator*: the schema has no rule comparing total with items; the save succeeds with the recomputed total.

excerpts.quote: body['subTotal'] = subTotal; body['taxTotal'] = taxTotal; body['total'] = total;

readMore.why: Trace 1: the data shape at each hop of invoice creation.

notes.title: The overpay guard answers 202
notes.body:
`paymentController/create.js` reloads the invoice with `Invoice.findOne({ _id, removed: false })`, computes `maxAmount` as total minus discount minus credit, and if `req.body.amount > maxAmount` returns `res.status(202).json({ success: false, ... message: 'The Max Amount you can add is ...' })`. A 202 ("accepted") status for a rejection is unusual; clients must read `success`.

- *A 400 from a Joi schema*: payment create has no Joi validation; the guard is a plain comparison.
- *A 200 with credit over the total*: the guard returns before `Model.create`.
- *A 409 conflict*: no 409 is used anywhere in this controller.

readMore.why: Trace 6: why the server re-checks what the client already checked.

notes.title: Three writes, no transaction
notes.body:
Payment create runs `Model.create(req.body)`, then a `findOneAndUpdate` to set the pdf name, then `Invoice.findOneAndUpdate` with `$push`, `$inc: { credit: amount }` and `$set: { paymentStatus }`. No session or transaction ties them together. If the process dies after the first write, the payment exists but the invoice's `credit`, `payment` list and status never change.

- *Mongoose undoes the create*: Mongoose has no automatic undo; a saved document stays saved.
- *An invoice marked paid with no payment*: the invoice update is the last write, so it is the one that is missing.
- *A pending payment and a retry job*: payments have no pending state and there is no retry job.

readMore.why: Flow B and the "what if the server crashes" question.

notes.title: A second delete finds nothing
notes.body:
`remove.js` calls `findOneAndUpdate({ _id: req.params.id, removed: false }, { $set: { removed: true } })`. For an invoice that is already soft-deleted the filter matches no document, so `deletedInvoice` is `null` and the controller returns `404` with "Invoice not found" before it reaches the payment cascade.

- *A 200 again*: the update never runs, because the filter excludes removed invoices.
- *A 500 from updateMany*: the null check returns first, so `updateMany` is never called.
- *A 410 Gone*: the controller only uses 404 and 200.

readMore.why: Trace 2: the soft-delete cascade and its consistency risk.

notes.title: Logout works through loggedSessions
notes.body:
A JWT cannot be cancelled once signed, so IDURAR keeps the issued tokens in `loggedSessions`. `logout.js` runs `$pull: { loggedSessions: token }`. On the next request `isValidAuthToken` verifies the signature (still valid), loads the user, and then checks `loggedSessions.includes(token)`; the token is gone, so it returns 401 "User is already logout".

- *jwt.verify after a secret rotation*: there is one `JWT_SECRET` from the environment; logout does not change it.
- *The exp claim rewritten*: a signed token cannot be changed by the server after it is issued.
- *None, until expiry*: that would be true of a plain JWT, but the session list check rejects it.

notes.title: An expired token gets a 500, not a 401
notes.body:
`jwt.verify(token, secret)` from `jsonwebtoken` throws `TokenExpiredError` for an expired token (and `JsonWebTokenError` for a bad signature); it does not return a falsy value. The `if (!verified)` 401 branch is therefore never reached for these cases. The throw lands in the `catch`, which returns `res.status(500)` with the error message and `jwtExpired: true`. The trace table lists "401 if bad" for this step; the code disagrees, and the code is what runs.

- *401 Token verification failed*: unreachable for expired or tampered tokens, since verify throws first.
- *401 No authentication token*: that branch runs only when the header has no token.
- *403*: the middleware never uses 403.

notes.title: Joi failures are answered in the controller
notes.body:
`schema.validate(body)` returns `{ error, value }`; it does not throw. `create.js` checks `if (error)` and returns `res.status(400)` with the first detail message itself. Nothing is thrown, so the `catchErrors` wrapper never sees it, and no save is attempted.

- *catchErrors after a thrown ValidationError*: that path is for Mongoose `ValidationError`s thrown by `save()`, which this request never reaches.
- *Mongoose validators*: the controller returns before `new Model(body).save()`.
- *The notFound handler*: it handles unknown routes; this route exists.

readMore.why: Trace 4: the Mongoose error path and its Verify question.

notes.title: The paid column is bound to credit
notes.body:
In `pages/Invoice/index.jsx`, the column whose title is `translate('paid')` has `dataIndex: 'credit'` and renders it with `moneyFormatter`. `credit` is the amount paid so far: payment create adds each payment's amount with `$inc: { credit: amount }`.

- *paymentStatus as an amount*: status has its own column and is a string such as `partially`.
- *Total minus discount*: that is what the invoice is worth, not what was paid; no column computes it.
- *A count of payment ids*: the `payment` array is not rendered in this table.

readMore.why: Trace 5: list rendering and money formatting.

notes.title: What setup writes before it crashes
notes.body:
`setup.js` runs in order: save the demo Admin, save its AdminPassword, then `Setting.insertMany` with every default settings file. Only after that does it `require('../models/appModels/PaymentMode')` and `Taxes`, which do not exist in this copy, so the require throws and the `catch` exits. The admin account and all default settings are already saved.

- *Nothing, one transaction*: there is no transaction; each save commits on its own.
- *Taxes but not PaymentMode*: both requires come before either insert, and the first one throws.
- *Only the password*: the Admin is saved first, before the password and the settings.

readMore.why: The two known landmines in this copy.

notes.title: A model file is enough for routes
notes.body:
`models/utils/index.js` globs `./src/models/appModels/**/*.js` and, for each file, derives the entity, model name and controller name into `routesList`. `appApi.js` loops over `routesList` and registers nine routes per entity (create, read, update, delete, search, list, listAll, filter, summary) wrapped in `catchErrors`. Convention, not configuration, creates the API.

- *Added by hand*: no per-entity routes are written in `appApi.js`; they come from the loop.
- *Mongoose registers routes*: Mongoose is a data layer; it knows nothing about Express routes.
- *Vite creates them*: Vite only proxies `/api` to the backend in development.

readMore.why: The first files to open, including where the entity list comes from.

notes.title: Page controls need the total count
notes.body:
The list thunk in `redux/erp/actions.js` builds `pagination.total` from `parseInt(data.pagination.count, 10)`. If the backend sends `count: result.length`, that is the size of the current page only, so the table believes there is just one page of results and paging breaks.

- *result.length equals the total*: only when everything fits on one page.
- *Sorting*: a count query does not sort; sorting is on the `find`.
- *Login*: the count has nothing to do with authentication.

notes.title: Hard deletes leave dangling payment refs
notes.body:
`Payment.invoice` is an ObjectId `ref: 'Invoice'` with `autopopulate: true`. MongoDB has no foreign keys and Mongoose adds no cascade, so `Invoice.deleteMany({ removed: true })` removes the invoices and leaves the payments pointing at ids that no longer exist. When those payments are loaded, autopopulate finds nothing and the field becomes `null`.

- *Deleted by a cascade*: no cascade exists for refs.
- *Reassigned to another invoice*: nothing rewrites payment documents.
- *Payments copy invoice data*: a payment stores only the invoice id; the rest comes from population.

excerpts.quote: type: mongoose.Schema.ObjectId, ref: 'Invoice', required: true, autopopulate: true,
